predecessors.note: 'After the Battle of Manzikert in 1071 the Seljuk army ... took possession of the city. Subsequently the Seljuks handed over control of the city to the Turkmen slave-commander Sökmen el-Kutbî' (Ahlat page); 'The Ahlatshahs were closely tied to Great Seljuq institutions' (Ahlatshahs page). The year of the handover is not given.

capitals.note: 'Sokman and his successors were known as the Shah-Armens or Ahlat-shahs and they made Ahlat their capital' (Ahlat page); 'In the year 1100 the Shaharmens captured Ahlat and made it the capital of their vast sultanate'.

rulers.note: 'The Ahlatshahs reached their brightest period under the fifty-seven-year reign of Sökmen II (1128-1185)'; he 'died without an heir in 581/1185' and 'the beylik was seized by a series of slave commanders after his death'.

rulers.note: 'condemning his principality to a period of instability that lasted until 1207' (Sökmen II page); the last Sökmenli ruler 'was killed by Tuğrulshah, the ruler (melik) of Erzurum'.

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe (Cliopatria lacks the Ahlatshahs). 'The Beylik was founded by the Sökmen el-Kutbî who took over Ahlat (Khliat or Khilat) in 1100'; the region 'comprised most of modern-day Bitlis and Van, and parts of Muş provinces', centred on Ahlat 'on the northwest shore of Lake Van'. The pages give no area or frontier, so the three provinces are drawn whole for the whole span; Muş is certainly over-drawn.

notes:
A state Cliopatria lacks (cliopatria_names []). Three pages opened (Ahlatshahs, Ahlat, Sökmen II), within budget. Wikidata id not obtainable: null.
Dates: the infobox gives 1071-1207 while the text gives 1100 for the capture of Ahlat; this dossier starts in 1100 (Ahlatshahs text, Ahlat page, Encyclopaedia of Islam as quoted). A sentence attributed to Toumanoff has the Ahlatshahs dispossessed 'by the Shah-Armen in 1189/1190', which reads against the page's own use of Shah-Armen for the Ahlatshahs and is not used. The Ahlat page says the Shah-Armen dominion 'lasted until the 30s of the thirteenth century up until the Mongol invasions', against 1207 on the other page; the 1207 Ayyubid takeover is the Ahlatshahs page's. Sökmen's end is not given (the founder's reign is not dated); the strip holds Sökmen II (1128-1185) and the instability to 1207 only.
Territory: 'most of modern-day Bitlis and Van, and parts of Muş provinces' (drawn as whole provinces; the Muş part is an over-draw) with no frontier, and a Georgian conquest in the twelfth century that reduced Ahlat 'to vassal dependency' (Ahlat page, undated, a suzerain-side event for the Kingdom of Georgia). The page also says the Ahlatshahs fought 'wars against Georgia in alliance with their neighbours to the north, the Saltukids' (undated): no war is recorded.
Mirrors: ayyubid-sultanate carries no 1207 gain (Ahlat 'taken over by the Ayyubids'); sultanate-of-rum has a 1230 gain of 'Erzurum, Ahlat, and the Lake Van region, which had been Ayyubid territory' from ayyubid-sultanate, consistent with the Ayyubid hold from 1207; the Ahlat page has Jalal al-Din capturing Ahlat in 1230 (khwarezmid dossiers).
Not settled: how the Seljuks handed Ahlat to Sökmen and when; the Eldiguzid suzerainty ('Ahlat ... became his vassals', Eldiguz page, undated: eldiguzids dossier); Malazgirt, Erciş and Adilcevaz, which the pages do not mention.
Gazetteer names used that it lacks: none.
